props.title: Fox and His Friends
props.initialSlug: Gay lottery winner exploited by ruthless lovers

sections.content: **Fox and His Friends** (1975) stands as one of Rainer Werner Fassbinder's most biting critiques of class exploitation in post-war Germany. The film follows Franz "Fox" Biberkopf, a working-class gay carnival worker who wins the lottery, only to be systematically stripped of his wealth by his sophisticated but manipulative upper-class lover. Fassbinder himself plays Fox with raw vulnerability, creating a devastating portrait of social climbing and betrayal. This film connects directly to other major LGBTQ+ classics like **Sunday Bloody Sunday** (1971) and The Bitter Tears of Petra von Kant (1972) in depicting complex queer relationships without making sexuality itself the central conflict.

sections.content: Fassbinder's unflinching examination of class warfare through a queer lens was revolutionary for 1975. While many gay films of the era focused on coming out narratives or tragic AIDS stories, **Fox and His Friends** presents its gay characters matter-of-factly while zeroing in on economic exploitation. This approach influenced later films like **My Beautiful Laundrette** (1985) and **Happy Together** (1997), which similarly explore how class and cultural differences impact queer relationships.

The film's visual style employs Fassbinder's trademark static compositions and mirror imagery to emphasize Fox's isolation and alienation. This aesthetic approach influenced later German cinema, particularly seen in works like **In the Year of 13 Moons** (1978) and contemporary films like **Head-On** (2004), which similarly use formal rigidity to express emotional devastation. sections.content: As a cornerstone of New German Cinema, **Fox and His Friends** exemplifies the movement's focus on social criticism and personal politics. Like Fassbinder contemporaries Werner Herzog with **Aguirre, the Wrath of God** (1972) and Wim Wenders with **Kings of the Road** (1976), the film confronts Germany's post-war identity crisis through intimate human drama rather than broad historical sweep.
